t.peak wilderness protected area@6.8,80.5:
At the heart of Sri Lanka's hill country rises a sharp cone of rock that Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians all hold sacred. Sri Pada, known to many as Adam's Peak, stands at 2,243 metres, and on its summit is a large depression in the rock shaped like a footprint. For Buddhists it is the footprint of the Buddha; for Hindus, of Shiva; for Muslims and some Christians, of Adam. The mountain lies within the Peak Wilderness Protected Area, a large expanse of montane forest that is part of the Central Highlands of Sri Lanka World Heritage site, listed in 2010.

The pilgrimage season runs from the full moon in December to the full moon in May, when thousands of people climb the steps to the summit, most of them at night to arrive in time for sunrise. The path from Dalhousie, the usual starting point, is lit and lined with tea stalls, and the climb takes several hours. At dawn, if the weather is clear, the peak casts a perfect triangular shadow across the clouds and the hills to the west. It is a magical experience, shared with families, monks and old pilgrims who have made the climb many times.

The forest around the peak is rich in wildlife, with endemic birds, monkeys and reptiles, and rivers that flow down to the lowlands. The lower slopes are covered with tea estates, a legacy of British colonial rule, with neat rows of bushes on steep hillsides and the colourful saris of the pickers.

Riding in the hill country is spectacular and demanding. The roads wind endlessly through tea estates and forest, with tight bends, steep gradients and narrow sections. Buses are the main hazard: they drive fast, overtake on blind corners and expect everything else to get out of the way. Surfaces vary, and landslides can block roads in the monsoon. Driving is on the left.

Hatton is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, shops and simple restaurants, and it is the gateway for Dalhousie. Fill up before heading into the hills. The weather is cool at altitude, and nights can be cold, so bring a warm layer for the climb. The southwest monsoon brings heavy rain from May to September; the pilgrimage season coincides with the drier months. Watch out for leeches on the forest trails.
t.rangiri dambulla cave temple@7.9,80.6:
The rock at Dambulla rises some hundred and fifty metres above the plain in the dry heart of Sri Lanka, a great bald dome of granite, and in its upper flank five caves hold one of the most extraordinary Buddhist shrines in Asia. Tradition says King Valagamba sheltered here in the first century BC when he was driven out of Anuradhapura, and that after regaining his throne he turned the caves into a temple in gratitude. Monks had been using them long before that, and kings went on adding to them for centuries.

Inside, the ceilings and walls are covered with painted murals in reds, yellows and ochres, flowing over every curve of the rock, and the caves are filled with statues of the Buddha, well over a hundred and fifty of them, standing, seated and reclining, along with figures of gods and kings. The largest cave stretches deep into the hill, and a spring drips from its roof into a basin that is said never to run dry. It is cool, dim and hushed after the glare outside. Remove shoes and hats at the entrance and cover shoulders and knees; the rock steps are hot by midday, so bring socks.

The climb up is a steady walk on stone steps with views over the forests and tanks toward Sigiriya, the famous rock fortress fifteen kilometres to the north-east, and the Knuckles range to the east. Macaques patrol the path and will open bags. At the bottom stands the modern Golden Temple, with a very large gilded Buddha on its roof, which is hard to miss and hard to love but marks the entrance.

Dambulla is a crossroads. The A9 runs north toward Anuradhapura and Jaffna and south toward Kandy, and the A6 heads to Trincomalee and the east coast, so traffic is heavy with lorries and buses, overtaking with remarkable confidence. Early mornings are cooler and calmer. The town is home to the country's largest wholesale vegetable market, and the trucks that come and go day and night carry produce from all over the island.

Fuel, food and guesthouses are plentiful in Dambulla. Stop for rice and curry at a roadside canteen, with half a dozen vegetable curries and fresh coconut sambol, or for a king coconut from a stall to cool off after the climb. Then ride on to Sigiriya in the afternoon light, or east into the Knuckles hills, where the roads get narrower, greener and far quieter.
t.pau brazil ceplac experimental station@-:
In April 1500, the Portuguese fleet of Pedro Álvares Cabral, sailing for India, sighted land on this coast and anchored near what is now Porto Seguro, in southern Bahia, making the first recorded European landfall in Brazil. The country took its name from the pau-brasil, a tree whose red wood was valuable for making dye and was exported in huge quantities in the early colonial period, nearly wiping it out. The CEPLAC experimental station near Porto Seguro, an agricultural research facility, lies within the Atlantic Forest reserves of this coast, listed by UNESCO in 1999 together with other protected areas of the Costa do Descobrimento.

CEPLAC is the Brazilian federal body for cocoa research, and southern Bahia was for a long time the heart of Brazil's cocoa industry, until a fungal disease, witches' broom, devastated plantations in the late twentieth century. The station protects a stretch of Atlantic forest, with tall trees, epiphytes and a rich wildlife, including rare birds and primates, and has contributed to the conservation of pau-brasil trees.

Porto Seguro is today a busy tourist town, with beaches, nightlife and a historic upper town, the Cidade Histórica, with colonial churches and a view over the sea. South of the town, across the river by ferry, Arraial d'Ajuda and Trancoso are laid-back beach villages with a bohemian atmosphere, set on cliffs above long beaches. To the north, Santa Cruz Cabrália has a monument marking the spot where the first mass was celebrated in Brazil.

For riders, the roads of southern Bahia are a mixed bag. The BR-367 links Porto Seguro to the BR-101, the main north–south highway, and roads along the coast connect the beach villages, some paved, others sandy or rutted. Traffic can be heavy in the tourist season, and speed bumps are frequent. The heat and humidity are intense, with heavy rains from April to July.

Porto Seguro, about fourteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants of every kind. Bahian food is rich and flavourful: try moqueca, a stew of fish or shrimp cooked in coconut milk and palm oil, or acarajé, a deep-fried bean fritter filled with spicy shrimp paste, sold by women in white dresses on street corners. And sit on the beach at sunset, with a fresh coconut, and think about the sailors who first saw this coast more than five centuries ago.
t.pau brazil national park@-16.5,-39.3:
Brazil is named after a tree. Pau-brasil, brazilwood, grew along the Atlantic coast when the Portuguese arrived in 1500, and its heartwood yields a deep red dye that was worth a fortune in Europe, so the early traders called the land after it. Within a few generations they had cut most of the coastal trees, and the species nearly vanished. Pau Brasil National Park, near Porto Seguro in southern Bahia, protects a patch of lowland Atlantic Forest where some of those trees still stand, with dense, humid woods, vines, palms and the bird calls of the tropics. The park is part of the Costa do Descobrimento Atlantic Forest Reserves, listed by UNESCO in 1999.

This is also the coast where Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet made landfall in April 1500, and the Pataxó people, who lived here long before, still live in villages nearby and share their crafts and stories. The ride list pairs the park with the national park at Descobrimento and Veracruz Station, so the whole area makes a day of forest and history.

Porto Seguro, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people, is a big resort city with fuel, hotels and a noisy nightlife, and Santa Cruz Cabrália, a smaller town of nearly twenty thousand, is quieter and has a pretty waterfront. The roads here are mostly flat, with long straight runs through plantations of eucalyptus, papaya and coconut, and the coastal highways, the BR-101 and the BA-001, are paved and busy with trucks, buses and holiday traffic. Watch for speed bumps, potholes and wandering dogs, and keep your speed sensible at night.

The climate is hot and humid all year, with showers at any time and a rainy peak from March to July. The drier months, from September to February, are the best for the forest and the beach, though the heat can be heavy at midday. Try moqueca, a fish stew in coconut milk, with tapioca crepes at breakfast, and cool off with fresh coconut water. A morning walk in the forest, before the heat, is the best way to see the trees.
t.sacred city of anuradhapura@8.3,80.4:
Anuradhapura was the capital of Sri Lanka for well over a thousand years, and it still feels like a capital of a certain kind, one made of brick, water and devotion. Standing in the dry zone, in the flat north-central plains, it grew from a settlement of the fourth century BC into the heart of a Buddhist kingdom that built huge dome-shaped dagobas, monasteries and reservoirs. The great tanks, or artificial lakes, were the engineering marvel that made rice farming possible in an area with scarce rainfall, and you can see several of them from the road, wide mirrors of water ringed with palms.

At the centre is the Sri Maha Bodhi, a fig tree said to have grown from a cutting of the tree in Bodh Gaya under which the Buddha reached enlightenment. According to the chronicles, the cutting was brought here in the third century BC by Sanghamitta, a Buddhist nun and the daughter of the emperor Ashoka, and the tree has been tended without interruption since. Pilgrims in white come to leave flowers and light lamps, and the atmosphere is calm. The giant dagobas, Ruwanwelisaya, Jetavanaramaya and Abhayagiri, rise like white hills, and the Jetavana was once among the tallest structures in the ancient world.

Dress and manners matter. You will be asked to cover your shoulders and knees, remove shoes and hats on sacred ground, and walk clockwise around the stupas, and it is the hot paving stones of midday that teach you to bring thin socks. Come early or late, when the light is gold and the heat is bearable.

For riding, the country around is flat and straight, with long, rather hypnotic roads running through paddy fields, scrub jungle and village after village. Traffic is the main hazard, with buses that overtake without hesitation, tuk-tuks, cattle and dogs, and monsoon rains can make surfaces slick. Anuradhapura is a good-sized city with fuel and plenty of rice-and-curry places. Mihintale, a hill to the east where Buddhism is said to have arrived on the island, makes a good short ride. The central highlands rise to the south, and the road to Kandy swaps the heat for tea terraces and cool mist.
t.veracruz station@-16.2,-39.1:
On 22 April 1500, a Portuguese fleet under Pedro Alvares Cabral anchored off this coast of Bahia, and the history of Brazil as a European colony began. The fleet was bound for India, and was blown far to the west, and the first mass in Brazil was held on shore a few days later. The area around Porto Seguro and Santa Cruz Cabralia is still called the Costa do Descobrimento, and the stretch of Atlantic Forest behind it is a UNESCO World Heritage listing, the Atlantic Forest Reserves of that same coast, one of the last pieces of lowland coastal forest in the north-east of the country. Veracruz Station is one of its protected areas.

The coast here is a long ribbon of white sand beaches backed by red cliffs and tall coconut palms, and behind it the forest rises in green layers. The forest is among the richest in the world in tree species, and holds many animals found nowhere else, including golden-headed lion tamarins, though you are more likely to see parrots, hummingbirds and butterflies. The Pataxo, the indigenous people of the region, still live in villages along the coast, and some welcome visitors to see their crafts and dances. It matters to approach such visits with respect.

The riding is easy and warm. The BR-367 and the coastal roads are flat or gently rolling, with palm groves and views of the sea, and the tarmac is usually good, though local roads can be patchy and there are many speed bumps in villages. Traffic builds in high season, from December to February, and at Carnival, and in July, and the best months are April to June and September to November. Rain showers can be sudden and heavy, and the heat and humidity are constant, so carry water and wear light riding gear.

Santa Cruz Cabralia, sixteen kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Porto Seguro, the main tourist town, has all the services. Food on the coast is excellent, with fresh seafood stew called moqueca, cooked in coconut milk and palm oil, tapioca pancakes and tropical fruits. Beach bars, called barracas, serve cold drinks and grilled fish, and a stop at one is a very good reason to park the bike for an hour.
t.ola a forest tract@19.5,-155.2:
Above the town of Volcano on the Big Island of Hawaii, the rain falls on a forest that has barely changed in a long time. The Ola'a Forest Tract is a patch of native rainforest on the flank of Kilauea, part of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, which together with the volcanoes Mauna Loa and Kilauea is a World Heritage site, inscribed in 1987. It sits at around 1,200 metres, where clouds drift in each afternoon, and the trees drip with moisture. The canopy is made of ohia lehua, a tree with brilliant red pom-pom flowers, and beneath it grow giant tree ferns called hapuu, with fronds that unfurl like croziers, and a thick understorey of native shrubs, mosses and orchids.

The forest is one of the best places in the islands to hear native birds. The apapane, a bright red honeycreeper, flits among the lehua blossoms, the iiwi, with its curved salmon-coloured bill, is sometimes seen, and in the early morning the forest fills with song. Many of the plants and birds found here live nowhere else on Earth, since Hawaii's isolation has produced species found nowhere else. Sadly, a fungal disease called rapid ohia death has killed many trees on the island, so visitors are asked to clean their boots and tyres before moving between forests.

The volcano road is a classic Hawaiian ride. Highway 11 climbs from Hilo through lush tropical forest up to Volcano, with the smell of wet earth and flowers, and Crater Rim Drive runs around the summit caldera of Kilauea with steaming vents and views over black lava fields. Parts of the park's roads have been closed after damage from earthquakes and eruptions, so check the park's website for current conditions. Rain is frequent at this altitude, so a waterproof layer is essential, and the roads are slick when wet. The temperature can be cool, and the early morning is often misty.

Volcano village has about twenty-five hundred people with a few shops and guesthouses, and for fuel and supplies you can go down to Mountain View or Hilo. The Hawaiian goose, the nene, grazes along the road, so watch for it, and keep your speed down.
t.discovery coast atlantic forest reserves:
In April of 1500 the Portuguese fleet under Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted a mountain on the Bahia coast, called it Monte Pascoal because it was Easter, and went ashore nearby. That is the usual start of Brazil's written history, and the stretch of coast around Porto Seguro and Santa Cruz Cabrália has been called the Costa do Descobrimento, the Coast of Finding, ever since. The Atlantic Forest reserves behind the beaches protect what is left of one of the most diverse and most reduced forests on Earth. Only a small fraction of the original Mata Atlântica remains, and the patches in southern Bahia are especially rich in plants and animals found nowhere else.

The coordinates sit inland from Porto Seguro, a city of about 120,000 people and the main base for fuel, food and rooms. The road network around here is dominated by the BR-101 and the BR-367, with smaller state roads leading toward the coast and the forest edges. Riding is easy but demanding in its own way: long straight stretches with lorries and buses, villages with speed bumps, and sudden potholes. Take care at dusk, when animals and unlit vehicles share the road. A shorter day with a detour to a forest road is better than trying to cover big distances.

The forest itself is humid and dense, with tall trees, epiphytes and orchids, and the soil smells of leaf mould. It is home to golden-headed lion tamarins and other primates, as well as a huge number of birds, though most visitors will mostly hear the forest rather than see it. The region is also known for its pau-brasil, the brazilwood tree that gave the country its name, and which was cut so heavily for dye in the colonial period that it became rare.

Ferries cross rivers near the coast, and in the rainy season dirt roads can become slippery or impassable, so ask locally before leaving the tarmac. The best months for riding are generally September to March, though rain is possible at any time. Porto Seguro has a lively historic upper town, Cidade Alta, with colonial churches dating from the sixteenth century, and a fresh moqueca, a Bahian fish stew cooked in coconut milk and palm oil, is the dish to look for. Carry water and sun protection, as the coastal sun is strong.
t.pokhara@28.2,84.0:
Pokhara is the point where Nepal's mountain drama starts to feel close. The city lies at about eight hundred metres, beside the long blue Phewa Lake, and from the lakeside you can see the Annapurna range lined up along the northern horizon, including the sharp summit of Machapuchare, the Fishtail, which has never been climbed because it is held sacred. On a clear morning the effect is almost unfair; on a hazy afternoon the peaks vanish altogether.

Around two hundred thousand people live here, and the town has grown from a trading stop on the old route between India and Tibet into the country's trekking capital. Shops sell boots, down jackets and maps, cafes serve momos and strong coffee, and boats paddle out on the lake to the small island temple. The World Peace Pagoda stands on a ridge above the water, reached by a steep walk or a short drive, and the view of the lake and the mountains is among the best here. Many Gurkha soldiers come from the hill villages of this region.

For riders, Pokhara is a hub. The Prithvi Highway from Kathmandu, about two hundred kilometres, winds along river gorges and through hill villages, busy with trucks and buses, and the journey can take six to eight hours. From here a road runs north along the Kali Gandaki, the deepest valley in the world by some measures, towards Jomsom and Upper Mustang, though the surface deteriorates quickly and the route demands care and experience. The monsoon, from about June to September, brings landslides and slick roads, so the best seasons are autumn and spring.

There is no shortage of fuel in Pokhara, with stations all around the city, and it is the place to fill up and check the bike before heading north. Spare parts and mechanics can be found, though not always for modern machines, so bring what you need. Water should be treated or bought sealed.

Aim to be on the lake for sunrise, when the mist lifts and the mountains turn pink. Then breakfast, a long ride, and as little rush as possible.
t.chitwan national park@27.5,84.3:
Chitwan is the lowland end of Nepal, a flat, hot and green country of river and forest that feels like a different nation from the mountains. The park, set up in 1973 as Nepal's first, lies along the Rapti and Narayani rivers in the Terai, and UNESCO listed it in 1984. It is a home for the greater one-horned rhinoceros, once close to extinction here, whose numbers have recovered thanks to strict protection, as well as Bengal tigers, gharial crocodiles with their long narrow snouts, sloth bears and hundreds of bird species.

The landscape is a patchwork of sal forest, riverine woodland and tall grassland that can reach over your head in autumn. The Tharu people, who have lived in the area for centuries and developed a natural resistance to the malaria that kept others away, run many of the lodges and guide services, and their villages of clay-walled houses with painted decoration are interesting in their own right. Most visitors stay in Sauraha, the main gateway on the northern edge of the park, where you can take canoe trips on the river, jeep safaris or guided walks.

Riding here is not about the park itself, as motorbikes are not allowed inside, but about the road getting you there. From Kathmandu the route follows the Prithvi Highway through river gorges and then drops into the plain, with the air getting warmer and denser. Traffic is heavy and unpredictable, with trucks, buses and wandering cattle, and the road passes through dusty towns. The best months are from October to March, when the weather is dry and cool, but fog can be thick in winter mornings. From April the heat becomes intense, and the monsoon from June to September brings flooding.

For fuel, the nearest larger town is Bharatpur, about twenty-two kilometres away, which has stations, shops, a hospital and an airport. Sauraha has basic provisions, but for the bike it is better to fill up before you arrive. Drink plenty of bottled water and carry insect repellent.

Be on the river at dawn, when the mist hangs over the water and rhinos wade in the shallows. It is worth the early start.
t.kandy@7.3,80.6:
Kandy is the heart of Sri Lanka's hill country, a city built around an artificial lake in a bowl of green hills at about five hundred metres. For over two hundred years it was the capital of the last Sinhalese kingdom, which held out against the Portuguese, Dutch and finally the British, who took it in 1815. Its great treasure is the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, the Sri Dalada Maligawa, which houses what is believed to be a tooth of the Buddha. The temple draws pilgrims every day, with drumming and offerings at set times, and the whole city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Around 110,000 people live here, so fuel, supplies and hotels are easy.

Each year, in July or August, the Esala Perahera takes place: a huge procession of drummers, dancers, fire performers and decorated elephants, which parades through the streets at night. It has been held for centuries and is one of the great festivals of Asia. Outside the festival, the town is busy and chaotic, and traffic around the lake is heavy, with tuk-tuks, buses and motorbikes competing for every gap. Left-hand traffic and a slow tempo are the rules, and you should not expect speed.

The ride out of Kandy toward the south and east climbs through tea country. Roads wind up the hills past Kadugannawa and Gampola, through plantations, villages and forest, and the air cools as you rise. The curves are tight, with blind corners, and buses and trucks often overtake at risky points, so keep to a measured pace. The surface is often patched, and rain, which can fall hard at any time, makes it slick. Early morning is the best time, with clear skies before the clouds build.

Sri Lankan food is a joy: rice and curry with a dozen small dishes, hoppers, which are bowl-shaped pancakes, and string hoppers for breakfast, plus strong tea grown in the hills. Ceylon tea was first grown commercially here in the 1860s, after coffee plantations were wiped out by disease. The Royal Botanic Gardens at Peradeniya, a few kilometres away, are among the finest in Asia. Leave early and enjoy the long climb into the cool.
t.nuwara eliya@6.9,80.8:
Nuwara Eliya is the town where Sri Lanka's tea planters and colonial officials tried to recreate an English country town, and the result is delightfully peculiar. It sits at nearly nineteen hundred metres in the hill country, in a bowl of green slopes below the island's highest peak, Pidurutalagala, and the air is cool and often damp. The architecture is a mixture of Tudor-style cottages with roses in the gardens, a red-brick post office, a golf course, a racecourse and a gentlemen's club with trophy heads on the walls. It earned the nickname Little England, and the locals have never quite let it go. The town was established in the 1840s, when the explorer and administrator Samuel Baker set up a settlement here, and became the favourite summer retreat of the British who ran the island.

The real reason to come is tea. The hills around the town are covered in tea estates, with their neat green rows, picking women in bright clothes and old factories where the leaves are withered, rolled and dried. Many estates are open to visitors, with tours of the factory and a cup of fresh brew in a tea room with a view. The tea grown here, at high altitude, is delicate, light and fragrant, among the best in Sri Lanka. In April, during the Sinhala and Tamil New Year, the town fills with Sri Lankan holidaymakers, there are horse races and a fair, and prices rise sharply.

The ride up is spectacular. From Kandy or from the lowlands, the road climbs through a series of hairpins, past waterfalls and tea slopes with wide views over the valleys. The roads are narrow, winding and busy with buses, trucks and tuk-tuks, so progress can be slow. The surface is generally paved but patchy, and in the wet months, mist and rain reduce visibility. Drive on the left, as in Britain, and be aware that local driving habits are assertive. Foreign visitors need a Sri Lankan temporary licence to ride legally.

Nuwara Eliya has everything for travellers. There are petrol stations in town, restaurants serving everything from rice and curry to scones and cream, hotels of all kinds and a lake with paddle boats. Evenings can be cold, so pack a warm layer. In the morning, fog often hides the hills, and then lifts to reveal a brilliant green.

Talawakele, about fourteen kilometres away, is a small town on the way down toward Colombo and a convenient service stop. The best months to come are January to March, when the weather is dry and clear.
t.horton plains@6.8,80.8:
Horton Plains is a high, windswept plateau in the middle of Sri Lanka, and nothing in the tropical lowlands prepares you for it. At more than two thousand metres, it is a land of rolling grassland, scattered patches of twisted cloud forest, tumbling streams and cool mist, and the air feels more like Scotland than the tropics. The plains are a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, part of the Central Highlands, and are home to species found nowhere else, including a number of endemic birds, orchids and the rhododendron that flowers in red along the paths. Sambar deer, the largest deer on the island, graze on the open grass, and leopards live in the forest, though they are rarely seen.

The great attraction is World's End, a sheer cliff where the plateau ends abruptly in a drop of nearly nine hundred metres to the plains below. On a clear morning, the view stretches to the southern coast, and on a very clear day you can see the sea. By ten o'clock, though, mist usually rises from the valley and fills the view with white, so it is essential to start early, ideally at dawn. A circular walking trail of about nine kilometres links World's End, a smaller drop called Mini World's End and Baker's Falls, a graceful waterfall in the forest. The trail is well marked and takes three or four hours at an easy pace.

The road to Horton Plains is part of a long climb through the hill country from Nuwara Eliya, past tea estates and small farms, and the highest section on the plateau is cool and often wet. The roads are narrow and winding, with a patchy surface and sharp bends. Fog and rain can come in quickly. Rules for vehicles in the park change, and entry is controlled with a ticket, so ask locally about what is allowed for motorcycles, and be ready to leave the bike at the gate and walk. The park is closed to cars and bikes beyond the entrance area in some seasons.

Nuwara Eliya, about nineteen kilometres away by straight line and further by road, is the main source, and Haputale, about sixteen kilometres in the other direction, has stations and shops. Bring food and water, since only basic refreshments are available at the gate. A rain jacket and warm layers are essential, because the temperature can fall close to freezing at night.

The silence of the plateau, broken only by the wind and the cry of birds, is one of its great charms. Stay on the trails, as the plants are fragile.
t.ella@6.9,81.0:
Ella is a small town on the edge of a huge drop, and the whole place has arranged itself around the view. It sits at about a thousand metres in the hills of Sri Lanka's Uva province, where the gap between two mountain ridges opens onto the plains to the south, and on a clear morning you can look straight through it and see the land falling away in layers toward the coast. Cafes and guesthouses line the main street, and the town has a relaxed, international travellers' feel, with banana pancakes on the menu and a stream of backpackers coming off the train from Kandy.

That train ride, one of the most beautiful in the world, is part of the Ella story. The line climbs through tea estates and forest to the highlands, and the blue carriages creep along on a steep gradient, with passengers hanging out of the open doors. A short walk from the town leads to the Nine Arches Bridge, a graceful stone viaduct built in the early twentieth century, which curves across a green valley. It is a striking structure, and watching the train cross it is a must for many visitors. Other short walks lead to Little Adam's Peak, a gentle hill with wide views, and to Ella Rock, a longer climb.

The ride out of Ella toward Wellawaya is the highlight for motorcyclists. The road drops through the Ella Gap in a series of hairpins, past Rawana Falls, a wide cascade beside the road, and into the hot, dry lowlands. The air changes from cool to warm within minutes, and the scenery from tea to scrub. The road is paved but narrow and used by buses and lorries, so caution is needed, and the surface can be slick after rain. In the other direction, the road to Badulla runs along a valley through tea and vegetable fields.

Ella has petrol stations on the main road, and there are plenty of small restaurants serving rice and curry, kottu roti and fresh juices. Badulla, about twelve kilometres away, is the larger town. Guesthouses range from basic to pleasant, with views over the gap, though prices rise in the high season from December to March.

Foreigners need a Sri Lankan licence to ride legally, and a temporary one is available through the authorities. The best weather is from January to March, though the area is lovely in any season if you accept some mist.
t.wellawaya@6.7,81.1:
Wellawaya is a junction town in the dry south-east of Sri Lanka, and its main claim to fame is that the road to the coast and the road to the hills part company here. Around ten thousand people live in the town, which sits on flat, scrubby land at the foot of the escarpment, with the Uva highlands rising behind. Ella and Haputale, both in the hills, are a short climb away, and the contrast is sharp: from cool tea terraces you drop through bends and waterfalls to a hot, flat plain dotted with palms, paddy and thorn scrub.

The descent from Ella to Wellawaya is a fine ride in its own right. The road drops steeply through a series of hairpins, passing the Rawana Falls, with a view over the plain that stretches to the horizon on clear days. The surface is usually fair, but buses and trucks take the bends wide, and monkeys and stray dogs wander onto the tarmac. Rain can arrive suddenly, and the monsoon months bring heavy downpours and some landslide risk on the upper section. In the early morning, mist often fills the valleys.

Just outside Wellawaya, at Buduruwagala, stand seven rock-cut figures of the Buddha and attendant bodhisattvas, carved into a cliff face, with the tallest around fifteen metres. They date back many centuries and are still in good shape, with traces of white, red and orange paint. The site is quiet, set among trees, and a nice place to stop. Further south lies Yala, one of the best parks for leopards, and Udawalawe, known for elephants, so the area is a gateway to wildlife as well as to the hills.

Wellawaya has fuel stations, banks, small restaurants and shops, and it is the largest settlement for some distance, so it is wise to fill up. Food is simple: rice and curry, kottu roti chopped on a hot griddle, and sweet tea. Heat is the main issue, since the plain is far hotter than Kandy, so drink plenty of water. The best months are January to March and July to September, which are drier, and the ride is rewarded by the long, cooling descent.
t.ancient city of sigiriya@8.0,80.8:
Sigiriya is a rock that looks like a fortress built by giants: a column of red granite rising some two hundred metres above the jungle of central Sri Lanka. In the late fifth century, King Kashyapa, who had seized the throne after killing his father, built a palace on its summit, with gardens, pools and fortifications around its base. The entrance was through the paws of a giant lion carved in the rock, of which only the paws remain. After Kashyapa's death, the palace was abandoned and became a Buddhist monastery. The Ancient City of Sigiriya was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1982.

The climb up the rock is steep, with stairs, iron walkways and narrow ledges. Halfway up, a sheltered gallery holds the famous frescoes of women, the Sigiriya maidens, painted with vivid colours, and the Mirror Wall, once polished so highly that the king could see his reflection, carries graffiti left by visitors over a thousand years ago. From the top, the view over the forest, lakes and hills is immense. Start early in the morning, before the heat and the crowds, and bring water.

Around the rock, the water gardens and terraced gardens are among the oldest landscaped gardens in the world. The area is also home to wild elephants, monkeys and many birds, and the nearby Minneriya and Kaudulla national parks are famous for the gathering of hundreds of elephants in the dry season.

Riding in Sri Lanka is an adventure. Traffic drives on the left, buses and tuk-tuks are aggressive, and dogs, cows and pedestrians wander onto the roads. Foreign riders need a local permit for their licence. Fuel is available in towns such as Dambulla, fifteen kilometres away, home to the Golden Temple cave complex, another UNESCO site. The Cultural Triangle, with Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa and Kandy, offers a wealth of history within a few hours' ride.
t.ancient city of polonnaruwa@7.9,81.0:
Polonnaruwa was the capital of Sri Lanka from the late tenth to the early thirteenth century, after the older capital at Anuradhapura was sacked, and its ruins are spread across a wide area of parkland beside a vast artificial lake. That lake, the Parakrama Samudra, was built by King Parakramabahu I in the twelfth century, and it is a testament to the ambition of the man who famously declared that not a single drop of rain should flow to the sea without serving people first. It still irrigates the paddy fields around the town today.

The ancient city is a mix of palaces, monasteries, audience halls and stupas, built in brick and stone. Highlights include the Vatadage, a circular relic house with beautifully carved guardstones and moonstones, the remains of Parakramabahu's royal palace, which once rose seven storeys, and above all the Gal Vihara, where four huge images of the Buddha were carved from a single granite outcrop, including a reclining figure fourteen metres long whose calm expression has moved visitors for centuries. Polonnaruwa was listed by UNESCO in 1982.

The area is warm, green and full of wildlife. Monkeys, both toque macaques and grey langurs, live among the ruins in large troops, and the national parks of Minneriya and Kaudulla to the west host huge gatherings of wild elephants in the dry season, especially from July to September. Elephants also cross roads in the area, particularly at night, and they are not to be trifled with; give them a wide berth and never ride towards one.

The roads here are a mix of decent main roads and narrow rural ones, shared with buses driven with heroic aggression, tuk-tuks, cyclists, cattle and dogs. Ride defensively, use your horn and do not ride at night if you can help it. The A11 links Polonnaruwa with Habarana, from where you can reach Sigiriya's rock fortress and the cave temples of Dambulla. The modern town has fuel stations, shops and simple restaurants, and rice and curry is everywhere and delicious. The heat is intense, so start early, rest at midday, and drink plenty of king coconut, sold at roadside stalls.
t.sinharaja forest reserve@6.4,80.5:
Sinharaja is the last large patch of primary lowland rainforest in Sri Lanka, a dense green world of towering trees, streams and constant dripping humidity in the south-west of the island. The name means lion king, though there are no lions; there are, however, leopards, purple-faced langurs, giant squirrels and an extraordinary number of species found nowhere else, especially birds, frogs and plants. It was listed as a World Heritage site in 1988, and ornithologists come from all over the world to see the mixed flocks that move through the canopy, with blue magpies, jungle babblers and drongos travelling together in noisy, colourful groups.

You will walk, of course, not ride, inside the reserve: entry is on foot with a local guide from the main entrances such as Kudawa on the north side or Deniyaya in the south. The forest is beautiful and demanding at the same time. The heat and humidity are intense, and leeches are almost guaranteed, especially after rain, so leech socks and a good repellent are worth their weight in gold. The rewards are waterfalls, enormous trees with buttress roots, and the feeling of being in a place that has hardly changed for millennia.

Riding in this part of Sri Lanka is a constantly changing experience. The roads to the reserve wind through tea and rubber plantations, small towns and villages, climbing up and down green hills, and they are often narrow, with surfaces that range from new asphalt to potholed and broken. Traffic drives on the left, and the private buses are the kings of the road: they overtake anywhere and expect you to get out of the way. Tuk-tuks, dogs, people and cows complete the picture. The south-west monsoon brings heavy rain from about May to September, and the second monsoon brings more later in the year, so the roads are often wet.

Ratnapura, the city of gems, is the nearest large town, about thirty kilometres away, with fuel, shops and accommodation, and its gem markets are a sight in themselves. The small towns closer to the reserve have basic shops and sometimes fuel, but it is better to fill up in Ratnapura. Eat a rice and curry in a local restaurant, often a dozen small dishes for very little money, and drink plenty of king coconut water against the heat.
t.central highlands of sri lanka@7.5,80.8:
North of Kandy the hills rise into a jagged massif that British surveyors thought looked like the knuckles of a clenched fist, and the name stuck: the Knuckles Range. It is one of the three parts of the Central Highlands World Heritage site, together with the Peak Wilderness and Horton Plains, and it is the wildest and least visited. The mountains are covered with montane forest, cloud forest at the highest points, grasslands and steep valleys with rivers and waterfalls. The weather changes fast; mist can sweep in over a ridge in minutes, and the air is noticeably cooler than in the plains. Many plants, frogs and lizards here exist nowhere else on Earth.

The road that makes this region famous with riders climbs from Matale through Rattota and up to Riverstone, a pass at the edge of the range. It is a steep, narrow road with a long series of hairpins, a crumbling edge in places and spectacular views over terraced valleys and the dry plains to the north. At the top, the forest closes in, and on a misty day the trees seem to drip with moss. Beyond Riverstone the road continues down towards Illukkumbura and the villages on the other side. Further south, Corbett's Gap offers another famous viewpoint, approached by smaller, rougher roads. Ride carefully: rain makes the surface slippery, and landslides happen.

The lowland approach is rich in history. Matale is a town surrounded by spice gardens, where you can see cinnamon, pepper, cardamom and nutmeg growing, and just north of the town is the Aluvihare rock temple, where, according to tradition, Buddhist monks first wrote down the Pali canon in the first century BC. Kandy, the last royal capital, with the Temple of the Tooth, lies to the south, and Sigiriya, with its rock fortress, is a good day's ride to the north.

Matale, about twenty kilometres away, is the town for fuel, shops and accommodation. Bring a jacket, even if it is warm in the plains, and leave early in the morning, when the views are clearest before the clouds build up.
t.monte pascoal national park@-16.9,-39.3:
On Easter Sunday 1500 the lookouts of Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet saw a rounded mountain rising out of the Atlantic haze and called it Monte Pascoal, Easter Mountain. A few days later the Portuguese landed on the coast nearby, and the story of European Brazil began. The mountain still stands over the low forested coastline of southern Bahia, and the national park around it protects some of the last stretches of Atlantic forest in this region. It is part of the Atlantic forest reserves of the Costa do Descobrimento, listed by UNESCO in 1999.

The park is also the homeland of the Pataxó people, who live in villages around its edge and have a long and sometimes difficult relationship with the park authorities. Visitors should respect the community and ask before entering their lands or taking pictures. Inside, the forest is thick with trees, bromeliads and orchids, with monkeys, birds and a few rarer animals, such as tapirs. The coast has long white beaches, mangroves and reefs, while the interior is a tangle of green.

The closest large town is Itamaraju, about thirty kilometres away, with nearly fifty thousand people, fuel and plenty of shops. The roads close to the park are a mix of paved highway and sandy or muddy tracks, and some become impassable in the rainy season, so check conditions locally and consider a guide. The BR-101, which runs inland of the coast, is busy with trucks, and the roads between the beaches and the park need care, especially after rain.

Heat and humidity are constant, with sudden heavy showers, so pack a rain jacket and drink plenty of water. The drier months, from September to March, are generally better, but coastal weather is unpredictable at any time. Seafood in the little coastal villages is wonderful, often a plate of fried fish with rice, beans and farofa, and the fruit juices, from cashew or passion fruit, are cold and sweet. The last light on the mountain is magnificent.
t.horton plains national park@6.8,80.8:
Horton Plains is a high, cool plateau in the central highlands of Sri Lanka, at around two thousand metres, and it feels a world away from the island's beaches and jungles. The ground is rolling grassland and patches of stunted cloud forest, wind-bent and covered in moss, with rhododendron and wild flowers at the edges. The air is thin and cold, and in the morning you may see breath and frost on the grass. Sambar deer graze in the open, and the park is home to many endemic birds and to rare small mammals, such as the Horton Plains slender loris.

The headline attraction is World's End, a sheer cliff where the plateau suddenly drops about nine hundred metres to the plains below. On a clear day the view runs all the way to the coast; but the cloud usually rolls in by mid-morning, so most visitors start early to catch the view. The walking route is a loop of around nine kilometres, with Baker's Falls along the way, and it is the only way to see the sights, since vehicles are not allowed beyond the entrance area. It is not a hard walk, but it is cold and wet at times, so bring a waterproof.

The journey to the plains is part of the pleasure. From Nuwara Eliya the road climbs through tea country, with hillsides stitched with neat green bushes, women pickers in bright clothes and thin waterfalls beside the road. The last part, from Pattipola, which has the highest railway station in Sri Lanka, is narrow and slow, and the mist, rain and potholes demand caution. The island's roads are busy with buses and tuk-tuks, so overtaking needs patience.

Nuwara Eliya, a town of around twenty-six thousand people, is the place for fuel, a cup of Ceylon tea and a meal; Haputale, on the southern edge of the hills, is smaller, but also a pleasant place to stay. Neither the park nor the gate sells petrol. January to March is the driest period, and the weather in the hills is unpredictable at any time of year. In this country of a thousand shades of green, the highland moor is a surprising change of scenery, quiet, windswept and empty.
t.discovery national park@-17.1,-39.3:
On the coast of southern Bahia, in the stretch of Bahia that Brazilians call the Costa do Descobrimento, a long beach of pale sand curves away beneath coconut palms and low cliffs, and inland the land rises to a green and misty ridge. It was along this shore, on 22 April 1500, that Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet sighted the round hill of Monte Pascoal, named for Easter, and the first sight of land in what became Brazil. The Pataxó people who lived on this coast met the Portuguese on the beach, and their descendants still live in the area, with some villages open to visitors who wish to learn about their customs and crafts.

The forest here is the Atlantic rainforest, of which only a small fragment remains, and the forest reserves along this coast were listed by UNESCO in 1999 for their rich plant and animal life, with high levels of tree diversity and many endangered species. Yellow-breasted capuchin monkeys, giant anteaters, sloths and a vast number of birds live in the forest, and the sea off the coast has humpback whales between July and November. I cannot tell you exactly what the park holds at this precise point, since access is limited, but the general character is a land of heat, humidity and green.

The drive is largely along BR-101, the great coastal highway, a busy road with heavy lorries, so the best riding is on the quieter side roads toward the beaches, where the surface can be patchy and sandy. The tropical climate means hot days and sudden showers, and the wettest months are March to July, while September to February is drier. Beware of livestock and the occasional pothole, and ride early in the day before the heat builds.

Prado, with fifteen thousand people, is a pretty beach town that was an important centre of the whaling and timber trades, and has restaurants serving moqueca, a fish stew with coconut milk and palm oil, and a good supply of fresh coconut water. Itamaraju, larger and further inland, has fuel and basic services, and both are the places to fill up. The ride continues north to the old station of Veracruz, a reminder of the days when a railway ran along this coast to carry timber.
t.sacred city of kandy@7.3,80.6:
Kandy sits in a bowl of hills in the middle of Sri Lanka, about five hundred metres above the sea, with a small artificial lake in the middle and the roofs of the Temple of the Tooth at its edge. The city was the last capital of the Sinhalese kings, who held out in the hills against the Portuguese, Dutch and then British for more than two centuries, until the British took it in 1815. The relic that gave the place its sanctity, a tooth said to be that of the Buddha, was brought to the island in the fourth century and passed from capital to capital, and has been kept in Kandy for centuries. The Sri Dalada Maligawa, its home, is white, gold-roofed and surrounded by a moat, and the evening drum ritual, with conch shells and chanting, is a moving thing to watch.

In July or August, the Esala Perahera fills the streets for ten nights with elephants in lamplit regalia, fire dancers, drummers and dancers, and the city's population swells. Outside that time Kandy is a busy place with a laid-back air, and the lake road, shaded by old trees, makes a pleasant walk. The Royal Botanic Gardens at Peradeniya, just outside town, were laid out on the grounds of a royal pleasure garden and have a famous avenue of palms and an orchid house.

The road up from Colombo, the A1, is part of the experience, though not an easy one. It climbs through Kadugannawa, where the old pass, engineered by the British in the 1820s, runs below a tall stone pillar, and the traffic on it is heavy, with long lines of buses and trucks overtaking on blind bends. Patience is needed, and riding at night is risky. Roads in the hills beyond, towards the Knuckles range and Nuwara Eliya, are far more fun, with tea estates and waterfalls, but they are narrow and often wet.

The monsoons matter. The south-west rains hit the hills from May to September, and the north-east from October to January, so the drier months from February to April are best, with March warm and clear. Leeches appear in wet forest, which is useful to know before stopping.

Fuel is easy in a city of over a hundred thousand and along the main roads, and small towns have pumps too. A cup of strong ceylon tea and a pastry in a lakeside cafe is a fair way to end the day.
t.old town of galle and its fortifications:
Galle Fort is one of those places where a wall tells you everything. The Portuguese were the first Europeans to build here, in 1588, but the Dutch, who took the town in 1640, turned it into the formidable stone fortress you see today, with bastions facing the Indian Ocean and a street grid laid out in the European manner. The ramparts run for nearly three kilometres around a small peninsula, and you can walk the whole circuit in an hour or two, looking down on the surf on one side and the red-tiled roofs on the other. A lighthouse, a Dutch Reformed church with grave slabs on its floor, and a clock tower give the town its landmarks.

The Fort was listed as a World Heritage site in 1988, and it is still lived in, with families, shops, small hotels and cafes in old Dutch merchants' houses. Walls and trees survived the tsunami of December 2004, which flooded the area, and the community has rebuilt a lively town. Galle is also a cricket city, with its famous ground just outside the walls, where the ocean breeze blows over the boundary rope.

For a rider, the interest lies in what is around. The coast road south and east of Galle runs along palm-fringed beaches, past fishing villages with stilt fishermen, and the Southern Expressway makes a fast run to Colombo. Your ride, however, heads inland and up to Horton Plains, a highland plateau more than two thousand metres above the sea, with cloud forest, grassland and a sheer cliff at World's End. The journey takes you from steaming lowland up through tea country, with the road tightening into bends and the air cooling noticeably as you climb. Buses and lorries in Sri Lanka drive fast and overtake in unexpected places, and traffic keeps to the left, so stay alert, and allow a long day.

Galle has fuel stations and plenty of places to eat, from simple rice and curry to fresh seafood, with wood-apple juice, hoppers and spiced cashews as accompaniments. The main seasons are December to April on this coast, with dry weather and calm seas, while the south-west monsoon, from May to September, brings heavy rain and rough surf. Early mornings are the coolest, and the walls make a good place to watch the sun come up.
t.hawaii volcanoes national park@19.4,-155:
Pele, the goddess of fire, is said to live in Halemaumau, the crater at the summit of Kilauea, and visitors who throw offerings into the steam do so with some seriousness. The Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, on the south-east side of the Big Island, covers two of the world's most active volcanoes: Kilauea, which has erupted on and off for centuries, and Mauna Loa, the largest active volcano on Earth, with a summit 4,169 metres above the sea and a base on the ocean floor far below. They are shield volcanoes, built of thousands of thin lava flows, and their slopes rise so gently that you hardly notice how high you are. The park is a World Heritage site, listed in 1987.

The landscape changes from the summit to the coast. Around the caldera, at about 1,200 metres, the air is cool and often damp, with ferns, ohia trees covered in red lehua flowers, and steam vents that curl from the ground. The Crater Rim Drive circles the caldera, passing the Thurston Lava Tube, a cave made by a lava stream that drained away, and parts of it have been closed or changed since the major eruption and summit collapse of 2018, so check what is open. The Chain of Craters Road then descends nineteen miles to the sea, across lava fields from different decades, black, cracked and bare, to a coast where waves crash against the lava cliffs.

For a rider, it is a joyous drive. The road from Hilo to the park on Highway 11 climbs steadily through rainforest and farmland, with good tarmac, gentle bends and a speed limit that is enforced. In the park, the roads are smooth and scenic, but speed limits are low and wildlife, including the endangered nene goose, may wander across the road. Weather changes quickly: rain showers are frequent, wind can blow cold at altitude, and fog may close in. Eruptions come and go, and the park may close areas because of volcanic gases or activity, so check the park's website before you set out.

Volcano Village, just outside the park entrance, has small shops and places to eat and stay, and Hilo, about forty-five minutes away, has the dependable fuel stations, so start with a full tank. Bring a rain jacket, a warm layer, water and sun protection. The coffee grown on the slopes of the Big Island, especially in the Kona and Kau districts, is a good reason to stop at a roadside stand. Dawn and dusk are the best times to see the glow of lava, if the volcano is active.
t.jomsom@28.8,83.7:
Jomsom is the main town of the Mustang district, strung along the bank of the Kali Gandaki river at about 2,700 metres, in what is often called the deepest valley in the world, because the river runs between Dhaulagiri and the Annapurna massif, both above eight thousand metres. The scale is hard to take in. Snow peaks hang on either side of the valley, the river bed is a wide plain of grey gravel braided with channels, and the town sits in the middle of it, a place of whitewashed buildings, apple orchards, and a small airport whose planes fly in only in the morning before the wind rises.

The wind is Jomsom's great character. Every afternoon, as the air heats on the Tibetan side, a strong wind funnels up the valley, strong enough to blow dust in your face and push a bike off line, and the locals plan their days around it. Ride early, when the air is calm and the light is clear, and be ready to shelter after midday. The wind has shaped the local culture, with houses built low and stone-walled, and prayer flags snapping in every gust.

The people here are mostly Thakali, an ethnic group known as traders and innkeepers, whose cooking is celebrated throughout Nepal, and the region is also a centre of Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage. Muktinath, a sacred site for both faiths, lies a short distance north-east, and pilgrims come from all over to visit it. The river bed itself holds a curious treasure: black stones called shaligram, which are ammonite fossils from the ancient sea that once covered this land, and which Hindus hold sacred. It is a reminder that these mountains were once seabed.

The road is not for the faint-hearted. In places it is little more than a track along the river, with stream crossings, loose gravel, landslides and washouts after rain, and it varies from season to season, so ask locally about conditions. Fuel is limited and sometimes hard to find, and when you do find it, it is expensive, so carry what you need and plan ahead. Food is simple and good: dal bhat, apple pie and apple brandy are local pleasures, and a warm room is welcome after the cold nights. Respect the altitude, and take it slowly.
t.kagbeni@28.8,83.8:
Kagbeni stands at 2,800 metres where the Jhong Khola stream joins the Kali Gandaki, and it is the last village before Upper Mustang, the old Tibetan-style kingdom of Lo, which was closed to foreigners until 1992 and still requires a special, costly permit. The village is a cluster of mud-brick houses, painted in earth reds and whites, huddled together with narrow lanes, covered passages and flat roofs stacked with firewood. Above it stands a red-walled monastery, Kag Chode, with its prayer wheels and low doorways, and the fields around are terraced and irrigated with water brought from the river by channels, a green patch in a landscape of grey and ochre.

It feels like the edge of the world, and in many ways it is. North of here the valley opens onto the dry Tibetan plateau, and the character of the land changes at once: bare cliffs eroded into fantastic shapes, caves cut into the rock, and a sky of astonishing clarity. The people are Tibetan in language and religion, and their houses, monasteries and customs are close to those on the other side of the border. Prayer flags and mani walls, which are long walls of stones carved with Buddhist mantras, line the paths, and you pass them on the left, as tradition requires.

The road that reaches here is tough going. It follows the river bed in places, crossing the stream, and can be blocked by water or rockfall. Wind is a daily event, strong enough to blow grit and stop you from keeping a line. The track beyond the village is rough, and for most riders the village is the end of the route. You will need to check the rules for riding in Upper Mustang, since permits, guides and regulations apply and change.

Jomsom, a short way south, has the nearest services, but even there, fuel can be hard to find. Food in the village is simple, with noodles, momos and tea, and guesthouses offer basic rooms with thick blankets. Apples, apricots and walnuts grow here, and in autumn the harvest is drying on the roofs. The nights can be freezing, so a warm layer is essential, and the altitude can cause headaches, so rest and drink water.
t.ghami@29.0,83.9:
Ghami is a village in Upper Mustang at about 3,500 metres, set among red and ochre cliffs on a high, windy plateau, and it is known for having one of the longest mani walls in Nepal. The wall runs for hundreds of metres along the edge of the village, a long ridge of stones carved with prayers in Tibetan script, and travellers pass it on the left, as is the custom, spinning the prayer wheels set into its length. The effect is striking: a wall of stone and colour, stretching across a bare landscape under a deep blue sky, built over centuries by people who believed each stone carried a blessing.

Everything here is Tibetan in style. The houses are flat-roofed and whitewashed with dark window frames, stacks of firewood and dried dung lie on the rooftops, and the barley fields are small and carefully walled against the wind. Upper Mustang was an independent kingdom until the 1950s, and its capital, Lo Manthang, lies further north, behind a high wall. The old royal line continued as a symbolic office until 2008. The monasteries here belong to the Sakya and Kagyu schools, with painted walls and old statues, and the paths between villages are lined with chortens.

The track through Upper Mustang is rough and slow, and in places little more than a line across gravel and stone. It crosses streams and passes along cliff edges, with a surface that changes with the weather. A motorbike here needs a good rider, spares and patience. The wind is relentless in the afternoon, and the altitude makes engines weak and riders tired, with thin air that catches the breath. Early mornings are calm and clear, and the light on the cliffs is spectacular. Check the rules for permits and routes, which apply to everyone and are enforced.

Do not expect to buy fuel or spares in Ghami. Villages here are small, and supplies are limited and costly, so carry what you need. Teahouses offer simple food, hot tea and dal bhat, and the owners are friendly. The nights are cold even in summer, and the days can be hot, so layers are the answer. The people here depend on herding, trade and a little farming, and the season is short, so be generous and respectful. Take plenty of water, go slowly, and let the place sink in.
t.mugling@27.9,84.6:
Mugling is a roadside town in the middle of Nepal, where the Prithvi Highway runs along the Trishuli river and the road to the plains meets the road to Pokhara. It is a place of passage rather than a destination, a gathering of tea shops, truck stops and small restaurants at a junction where drivers stop to eat, check their loads and talk. The Trishuli river is green and fast here, and the hills rise steeply on both sides. Mugling sits at the point where the river meets the Marsyangdi, and the junction has always been a crossing place for travellers between Kathmandu, the lowlands and the mountains.

The highway was built with Chinese help in the early 1970s, and it is the main road linking Kathmandu and Pokhara, two of Nepal's most important places. Trucks, buses and cars grind along it day and night, and a rider needs to be alert. The road is paved but often narrow and patched, and in the monsoon landslides can cut it for hours or days. Lorries overtake in places where you would not, and buses sound their horns constantly. Ride defensively, watch for loose gravel on bends, and avoid the road at night.

The restaurants at Mugling are known for their food. Truck drivers and bus passengers stop for dal bhat, a plate of rice, lentils and vegetables that is refilled until you say stop, and for fried fish from the rivers, grilled and spiced. It is cheap, filling and good, and an ideal break on a long day. Tea is sweet and milky, made with spices, and you can drink it standing at a stall with the engines idling around you.

Fuel is easy here, as this is a busy highway town, with several stations. Bharatpur, about twenty-three kilometres south, is the nearest big city, with more than a hundred thousand people, and has everything from hospitals to workshops. Be careful of water quality, and stick to bottled water and cooked food. The best time to travel is the dry season, from October to April, when the air is clear and the road in better shape. The monsoon brings heavy rain, mud and delays, and a motorbike on this road in July is a test of nerve.
t.bandipur junction@27.9,84.4:
Bandipur junction is a roadside turn on the Prithvi Highway, in the settlement usually called Dumre, where a side road leaves the busy highway and climbs to Bandipur, a hill town that feels like it belongs to another century. The highway here is a noisy, dusty ribbon of trucks, buses and shops, with roadside stalls selling oranges and fried snacks. The side road is a short, steep climb of about eight kilometres, with hairpins through terraced fields and forest, and at the top, at around a thousand metres, the air is cooler and quieter.

Bandipur was a trading town of the Newar people, who built a long bazaar of tall, stone-faced houses with carved wooden windows and slate roofs, and who grew rich on the trade between India and Tibet. When the highway was built in the 1970s, traffic bypassed the town, and the trade collapsed, which was a blow to Bandipur but a gift to its architecture, which was left intact. Today the main street is car-free, paved with stone, and lined with guesthouses, cafés and small shops. From the edge of the ridge, a viewpoint looks out over the valley to the Himalaya, and on a clear morning the snow peaks of the Annapurna and Manaslu ranges stand in a line along the horizon.

For a rider, the climb is easy and pleasant. The road is narrow and has a patchy surface, with the occasional pothole, and the hairpins are short and tight, so take care on the wet or dusty bends. Traffic is light, apart from local buses and the odd jeep. At the top, you park outside the town and walk in. If you have time, stay the night, because the evening light on the bazaar, the smell of woodsmoke and cooking, and the stillness after dark are worth it.

Fuel is available on the highway at Dumre, before you climb, and Bharatpur, the large city about twenty-nine kilometres away, has everything else. Bandipur has simple restaurants serving dal bhat, momos and Newari dishes, and a cup of tea at the viewpoint is a real pleasure. A cave, Siddha Gupha, lies below the town, and is a short walk for the curious. Bring a warm layer for the evening, and a torch.
t.mauna kea access road junction@19.8,-155:
Nobody tells you how empty the middle of Hawaii is. The Saddle Road runs between two enormous volcanoes, Mauna Kea to the north and Mauna Loa to the south, across a high plateau of lava, scrub and cloud, and the access road to the Mauna Kea visitor station leaves it at a junction that is easy to miss. There is no town, no cafe, just a turning and a ridge of dark cinder cones. Everything on this island looks smaller than it should, because the mountains are so large that they do not look like mountains at all.

The road itself, officially the Daniel K. Inouye Highway, was rebuilt in the 2000s and is now a smooth, fast and rather lovely ride. Long, open curves cross old flows, with views of Mauna Loa's gentle dome and, on clear days, of the white observatory domes on the summit of Mauna Kea. At around 2,000 metres the air is thin and cool, and cloud rolls in and out in minutes, so do not be surprised by wet tarmac, dense fog, and drifting mist on an otherwise sunny day. Nene, the Hawaiian goose, wander near the road in places. There is also a military training area near here, so you may meet convoys.

The side road climbs to the Onizuka visitor information station at roughly 2,800 metres, where people acclimatise before the summit. Above that, the road becomes steep gravel, with a ban on most rental vehicles and a firm warning against it for anything that is not well prepared, so I would treat the visitor station as your destination and the summit as someone else's adventure. Mauna Kea is sacred to Native Hawaiians, and the summit has been a site of long-running dispute over telescope construction, which is part of what you are looking at.

Do not run low on fuel in this part of the island. There are no stations along the Saddle Road itself. Waimea, about 37 kilometres to the north, is the closest town with a proper range of shops and petrol, and Hilo and Kona are the other ends. Rental agreements sometimes restrict the road, so check the paperwork. Bring a jacket, because it is far colder than the beaches you left behind.
t.saddle summit@19.8,-155.6:
At 2,020 metres, the high point of the Saddle Road is a spot where the Big Island makes you feel its scale. You are on a broad, tilted plateau between Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa, and everything around you is volcanic: black lava from flows within recent human memory, scrubby grass, a few pale ohia trees, and a sky that can be absolutely blue or absolutely gone, depending on which minute you arrive.

The road here is the island's great cross-country route, and for years it was notorious. Rental companies forbade it, the surface was narrow and broken, and the military used it more than tourists did. The modern highway is a different animal. It was rebuilt into a wide, smooth road with good sight lines, and bikers now use it as a fast, easy way to go from Hilo to the Kona side. The curves are gentle and the camber is kind. The conditions are the challenge: strong crosswinds off the volcano slopes, sudden banks of cloud, and in the early morning a cold that bites through a summer jacket. Wet patches, sometimes slick, appear in the shade.

What is interesting is the geology. Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth by volume, and its flows have come close to this road more than once, most recently in the 2022 eruption, which sent lava toward the highway before it stopped. You are riding across ground that is, by geological standards, not finished yet. The older Mauna Kea, to the north, is dormant, and its flanks hold the astronomical observatories. Pohakuloa, the large military training area nearby, explains the occasional convoy and the sign for unexploded ordnance off the road. Stay on the pavement.

Waimea is the nearest decent-sized town, about thirty kilometres away, with petrol, food and a very different, cattle-ranch feel at the edge of the hills. Hilo to the east and the Kona coast to the west also have everything. Bring warm kit even if the beach was hot, and expect to feel slightly breathless if you hike anywhere.
t.mauna loa and kilauea volcanoes@19.3,-15:
Hawaii's Big Island is still being built, and here you can stand on the evidence. Mauna Loa rises to about four thousand two hundred metres above sea level and is the largest active volcano on Earth by volume, while Kilauea beside it has been one of the most active, with eruptions that have repeatedly reshaped the south-east coast. The two together form the heart of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, which is a World Heritage site. Mauna Loa itself woke in 2022 after thirty-eight years of quiet, a reminder that the mountain is not a museum piece.

The riding is more varied than people expect. From the south-west side, the Hawaii Belt Road, or Highway 11, climbs from the ocean through macadamia and coffee country into cool upland forest. Around the park, Crater Rim Drive circles the summit caldera of Kilauea and Chain of Craters Road drops almost nineteen miles down to the sea through old lava flows, with long open bends and a view of black rock meeting white surf. In the highlands it can be misty and wet, and temperatures drop sharply, so bring a rain layer. The air near vents can carry volcanic gas, known locally as vog, which is a problem for people with breathing issues, and some roads and trails close when conditions turn dangerous. Check the park's current status before heading out.

Hawaiian tradition honours Pele, the goddess of volcanoes, who is believed to live in Halemaʻumaʻu, the crater at Kilauea's summit. Rangers and local people will tell you that it is respectful not to take lava rocks away, and there are plenty of stories about luckless tourists who mailed them back. The landscape is unforgettable: steam rising from the ground, fields of ropey pahoehoe lava, ferns pushing up through cinder, and the endangered nene, Hawaii's state bird, wandering near the roadside.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Pāhala and Volcano village have small supplies, but the larger towns are Hilo to the north-east and Kailua-Kona on the other coast, both a long drive away. Fill up wherever you pass a station, bring water and food into the park, and plan for rain and cool temperatures even if the lowlands are hot.
t.knuckles conservation forest@7.5,80.8:
The Knuckles range gets its name from a row of peaks that, seen from the Kandy side, look like the knuckles of a clenched fist. It rises in the central hills of Sri Lanka, northeast of Kandy, between the dry plains and the wet highlands, and it is cloaked in forest that changes with height from dry scrub to cloud forest, wet montane woods and grassland on the tops. Matale, about twenty kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, and Kandy lies not much further.

The forest is a haven for wildlife. Leopards, Sri Lankan elephants at the edges, purple-faced langurs, endemic frogs and lizards, rare orchids and countless butterflies live here, and the mist that settles on the ridges feeds waterfalls and streams. In 2010 UNESCO included the Knuckles area in the Central Highlands World Heritage listing. Villages such as Meemure, famously remote, were reachable only on foot until quite recently, and still feel like a different world.

The roads are another matter: narrow, steep and twisting, often with a patchy surface and hairpins that can be unpaved or washed out after heavy rain. They are also glorious, with views over tea estates, paddy terraces and valleys filled with mist. The climb from the plains passes through spice gardens of cardamom, pepper and cocoa. Riders should take care with landslides and with buses and trucks that take the whole road, and should not expect help if a bike breaks down.

The south-west monsoon, from May to September, brings heavy rain to the western side, and the north-east monsoon, from October to January, affects the eastern slopes, so the weather is rarely fully dry. Leeches are active in the wet and walkers should carry salt or repellent. Fill up in Matale or Kandy, as petrol is scarce in the hills. A simple lunch of rice and curry in a small restaurant, with tea from the estates, is the right ending.
t.lo manthang@29.2,84.0:
Lo Manthang is a walled city on a high, windy plateau in the north of Nepal, close to the Tibetan border, and it was the capital of the old kingdom of Lo, which survived as a semi-independent state until 2008. The city lies at about 3,800 metres on the dry side of the Himalaya, in the rain shadow of the Annapurna and Dhaulagiri ranges, and the landscape is a desert of eroded cliffs, red, ochre and grey, cut by the deep gorge of the Kali Gandaki river. The area was closed to outsiders until 1992, and permits are still required and costly. The people are of Tibetan origin, and the culture, language and religion are Tibetan Buddhist.

The walled city is a maze of whitewashed mud-brick houses, flat roofs stacked with firewood, narrow lanes and ancient monasteries. The walls, about six metres high, enclose a space of less than a square kilometre. The royal palace, a five-storey building, stands at the centre, and the monasteries, such as Jampa Lhakhang and Thubchen Gompa, hold wall paintings that date back to the fifteenth century and are among the finest of their kind. Restoration work has been carried out by international teams, and photography is restricted in some temples.

The road to Lo Manthang follows the Kali Gandaki, an old trade route for salt from Tibet and grain from Nepal, and it is a rough dirt track, with river crossings, landslides and steep sections. It is not a road for a standard bike: expect rocks, sand, washouts and wind, and strong winds blow up the valley in the afternoon, so travel in the morning. The weather is dry, and the season runs from March to November, with the monsoon barely reaching this area. Cold nights and strong sun make layers essential.

There are no real fuel stations, and supplies are brought up from Jomsom, a long way south, so riders carry extra fuel and parts. Guesthouses in the city serve dal bhat, tsampa and butter tea, and the Tiji festival, held in spring, with masked dances in the courtyard of the palace, draws visitors. Altitude is a serious matter, and acclimatisation is important. The wind, the dust, and the sense of arriving at a place that time has barely touched, make this journey memorable.
t.hilo@19.7,-155.1:
Rain is the first fact about Hilo. The town gets well over a hundred inches a year, making it one of the wettest cities in the United States, and the rain is what turned this side of the Big Island into a lush tangle of ferns, orchids, bamboo and waterfalls. Hilo is a low, tidy, slightly faded town of forty thousand people curved around a bay, with old wooden shopfronts, a farmers market that sprawls across several blocks, and the vast shoulder of Mauna Kea rising unseen behind its cloud.

It has been rebuilt more than once. Tsunamis hit the bay in 1946 and 1960, killing many people and wiping out the waterfront, and the old bayfront district is now a park, with a museum recalling the disasters. The town is a good place to eat, with Japanese, Filipino, Portuguese and Hawaiian influences all in the kitchen: saimin noodle soup, loco moco, malasadas, poke. Nearby, Rainbow Falls drops into a pool under a lava rock arch, and, when sun slants through the mist, they live up to their name.

Saddle Road begins here. Officially renamed for a late senator, it crosses the high saddle between the two giant volcanoes, Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa, both rising above thirteen thousand feet. For years it was a rough, narrow track that rental car companies banned, but modern rebuilding has turned it into a fast, smooth road with long bends and wide views. The road climbs from the wet tropics through ranchland and into a high lava desert, passing the turn for the Mauna Kea visitor station, and the climate changes with every few miles.

Prepare for the swing. Hilo can be warm and drizzly, and up on the saddle it can be cold, windy and foggy, so carry layers and a rain jacket. The road is also busy with trucks and has convoys from the military training area at Pohakuloa, and clouds can obscure the road in a flash. Early morning is usually the clearest time, before cloud builds up over the volcanoes.
